name: Predynastic period (Egypt)
other_names: Naqada period (Upper Egypt); Neolithic and Chalcolithic Egypt
making_significance: Naqada and Lower Egyptian communities made painted pottery, stone vessels, palettes and ivory work that set the craft base of the pharaonic state.
defined_by: Egyptologists (Petrie's sequence dating, refined by Kaiser and Hendrickx)
leaves_out: Nubian and desert neighbours; the unnamed village makers
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Early Dynastic Period (Egypt)
making_significance: The first dynasties organised royal workshops for stone vessels, copper tools, ivory and furniture found in the royal tombs at Abydos and Saqqara.
defined_by: Egyptologists (Manetho's dynasties as modern chronological units)
leaves_out: non-royal Egyptians and the retainers buried with kings
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Old Kingdom (Egypt)
making_significance: State-organised crews quarried, moved and dressed stone for pyramids, while tomb workshops produced statuary and relief on a new scale.
defined_by: Egyptologists; the term was set in 19th-century German Egyptology (Bunsen)
leaves_out: the workers' own view, known from Giza workers' town and graffiti of crews
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: First Intermediate Period (Egypt)
making_significance: With royal power divided, provincial workshops made their own styles of coffins, stelae and models.
leaves_out: the provincial makers the "decline" label devalues
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0)
notes: "Intermediate" frames it as a gap; many scholars now stress regional creativity.

name: Middle Kingdom (Egypt)
making_significance: Middle Kingdom workshops produced jewellery, block statues and coffins that later Egyptians treated as a classical model.
leaves_out: Nubians under Egyptian fortress control
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0)

name: Second Intermediate Period (Egypt)
making_significance: Hyksos rulers in the Delta and Kerma power to the south brought horses, chariots and Levantine bronze-working into Egypt.
leaves_out: the Levantine and Nubian people cast as invaders
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: New Kingdom (Egypt)
making_significance: Royal and temple workshops, and the village of Deir el-Medina, produced tomb painting, glass, faience and furniture for an imperial state reaching from Nubia to the Levant.
leaves_out: captive and tribute labour from Nubia and the Levant
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Amarna period (Egypt)
making_significance: Akhenaten's court at Amarna changed royal art, and the excavated workshop of Thutmose shows how portrait sculpture was made.
leaves_out: the Amarna workers' cemeteries, which show hard labour
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Third Intermediate Period (Egypt)
making_significance: Divided rule by Libyan and Kushite dynasties saw fine bronze statuary and reused tomb goods.
leaves_out: Libyan and Kushite rulers labelled as foreign
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Late Period (Egypt)
making_significance: Saite rulers revived Old Kingdom styles, and workshops mass-produced bronze votive figures and animal mummies.
leaves_out: the Persian rulers of Egypt, often erased from narratives
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0)

name: Ptolemaic period (Egypt)
making_significance: Greek and Egyptian workshops worked side by side, making temples in Egyptian style and Alexandrian glass, faience and portraits.
leaves_out: the Egyptian majority behind Greek-centred accounts
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Roman and Byzantine Egypt
making_significance: Egypt supplied grain and made linen, papyrus and painted mummy portraits, and later Coptic textiles.
functions: clothing and adornment;record and writing;ritual and belief
leaves_out: the rural population known mainly through tax records
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons
notes: links: POL120; STY083. "Coptic period" is a contested alternative label.

name: Napatan period (Kush)
making_significance: Kushite kings at Napata built pyramids and temples and made bronze, gold and faience in forms that blended Egyptian and local traditions.
leaves_out: Nubian self-definition beyond Egyptian models
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Meroitic period (Kush)
making_significance: Kushite rulers based at Meroë smelted iron, wrote in Meroitic script and made painted pottery and gold jewellery.
leaves_out: Meroitic, still only partly read
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Medieval (Christian) Nubian period
making_significance: Christian kingdoms of Nobadia, Makuria and Alwa painted church murals, made manuscripts and fine painted pottery.
leaves_out: Nubian Muslims and the gradual change after 1300
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Earlier Stone Age (Africa)
date_note: approx.; ends at different times by region
making_significance: The ESA covers the earliest known stone tools, from Lomekwian and Oldowan flakes to Acheulean hand axes.
defined_by: Goodwin and van Riet Lowe (1929) for southern Africa
leaves_out: the hominin makers who were not Homo sapiens
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports; Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where designated)
notes: links: ARC001; ARC002; ARC003; INV139; INV140.

name: Middle Stone Age (Africa)
date_note: approx.; ends regionally c. 50,000–25,000 years ago
making_significance: The MSA saw prepared-core tools, ochre use, shell beads and engraved pieces associated with early Homo sapiens.
leaves_out: the Eurocentric "Upper Palaeolithic revolution" frame it challenged
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports
notes: links: ARC004. Period row; ARC004 is the technocomplex.

name: Later Stone Age (Africa)
date_note: approx.; start c. 50,000–20,000 years ago by region; continues into the recent past
making_significance: The LSA covers microlithic tools, ostrich-eggshell beads and rock art made by hunter-gatherers, in some places into the 19th century.
leaves_out: the living San and other descendants, framed as "prehistoric"
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports
notes: links: ARC009. The ESA/MSA/LSA scheme was built to avoid European terms.

name: African Humid Period
date_note: approx.; end time-transgressive, c. 6,000–4,500 years ago
making_significance: A wetter Sahara supported fishing, herding and early pottery, and its drying pushed people towards the Nile and the Sahel.
leaves_out: regional variation hidden by one label
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access journals (DOAJ, SciELO, Persée)

name: Pastoral period (Saharan rock art)
making_significance: Paintings and engravings of cattle herds and camp scenes record herding life in the green Sahara.
leaves_out: the herders' own descendants and regional variation
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; open-access excavation reports

name: Camel period (Saharan rock art)
making_significance: Images of camels and Tifinagh inscriptions mark the camel's arrival in the Sahara and the trans-Saharan routes.
leaves_out: the Tuareg and other living descendants
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; open-access excavation reports

name: Early Iron Age (eastern and southern Africa)
date_note: c. 500 BCE in the Great Lakes; c. 200–1000 CE in southern Africa
making_significance: Farming communities smelted iron, made comb-stamped pottery and kept cattle, associated with Bantu-speaking expansions.
leaves_out: foragers who were already there; the language labels
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Later Iron Age (southern Africa)
making_significance: Later farming states such as Mapungubwe and Great Zimbabwe built stone enclosures, worked gold and traded to the coast.
leaves_out: oral histories of the descendant communities
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports; Zamani Project (link-out)

name: Aksumite period
making_significance: Aksum made stone stelae, gold coins with Ge'ez inscriptions and churches, trading via Adulis.
leaves_out: the pre-Aksumite and later Ethiopian periods
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Gondarine period (Ethiopia)
making_significance: The royal capital at Gondar built castles and churches and supported painting in a distinctive "Gondarine" style.
leaves_out: non-Amhara Ethiopians
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; British Library Endangered Archives Programme

name: Atlantic era (West and Central Africa)
making_significance: European ships brought cloth, beads, metals and guns, and the trafficking of enslaved people reshaped states, crafts and trade in West and Central Africa.
leaves_out: African agency, seen too often only as reaction
free_sources: SlaveVoyages (historical data public domain); PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out)

name: Mfecane
making_significance: A period of wars and migrations in southern Africa is linked with the rise of the Zulu kingdom, though the term is contested.
leaves_out: colonial and slave-raiding pressures
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out)

name: Colonial period (Africa)
making_significance: Colonial rule brought mission schools, forced labour and new markets that shaped carving, weaving and metalwork.
leaves_out: African continuities through the period
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out)

name: Nahda
making_significance: The Arabic cultural revival brought printing, journals and new styles of type and design.
leaves_out: non-urban and non-elite Arabs
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Digital Library of the Middle East

name: Ubaid period
making_significance: Ubaid villages made painted buff pottery, clay sickles and mud-brick temples that spread from southern Mesopotamia to the Gulf.
defined_by: Near Eastern archaeologists (named after Tell al-'Ubaid; 1930 Baghdad conference)
leaves_out: the Gulf coast communities treated as periphery
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); open-access excavation reports
notes: links: ARC053. Period row; ARC053 is the culture.

name: Uruk period
making_significance: Uruk-period cities used mass-produced bevelled-rim bowls, cylinder seals and the first proto-cuneiform tablets to organise labour and goods.
leaves_out: the workers paid in rations
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (link-out); Met Open Access (CC0)
notes: links: ARC054; HOR010; INV001; INV172. Ration labour flagged as human-flow.

name: Early Dynastic period (Mesopotamia)
making_significance: Sumerian city-states made the Royal Tombs of Ur's gold, lapis and shell inlay work, votive statues and inscribed monuments.
functions: ritual and belief;rule and display;play and music
leaves_out: the retainers buried in the Ur royal tombs
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (link-out); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Akkadian period
making_significance: The Akkadian kings commissioned victory stelae, cast copper heads and fine seals.
leaves_out: the conquered cities
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (link-out); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Ur III period
making_significance: Ur III kings ran state textile and craft workshops recorded on tens of thousands of tablets.
leaves_out: the women weavers and dependent labourers in the tablets
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (link-out)

name: Old Babylonian period
making_significance: Hammurabi's Babylon issued a law code with wages and liability for builders and craftsmen.
leaves_out: the enslaved people named in the code
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (link-out)

name: Kassite period
making_significance: Kassite rulers made glass, moulded brick facades and boundary stones (kudurru).
leaves_out: the Kassite language and origins
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (link-out)

name: Neo-Assyrian period
making_significance: Assyrian palaces were lined with carved reliefs and filled with ivory furniture, much of it taken as tribute and booty from Levantine workshops.
leaves_out: the craftsmen, including deportees, and the Levantine workshops whose ivories came as tribute and booty
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (link-out)

name: Neo-Babylonian period
making_significance: Neo-Babylonian kings rebuilt Babylon with glazed-brick gates and processional ways such as the Ishtar Gate, using deported craftsmen among others.
leaves_out: the Judaean and other deported communities
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Middle Elamite period
making_significance: Middle Elamite kings built the ziggurat at Chogha Zanbil and made glazed bricks, bronze statues and glass.
leaves_out: the builders of Chogha Zanbil
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Iron Age I–III (western Iran)
making_significance: The sequence covers grey-ware cemeteries, Hasanlu's gold bowl and the Luristan and Marlik bronzes.
defined_by: archaeologists (T. Cuyler Young Jr, 1965; Dyson at Hasanlu)
leaves_out: objects looted from unrecorded sites
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); open-access excavation reports

name: Chalcolithic (Southern Levant)
making_significance: Makers in the Southern Levant cast complex copper objects by lost wax, as in the Nahal Mishmar hoard, and made ivory figurines and churns.
leaves_out: the herders and villages outside the big sites
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports; Wikimedia Commons

name: Early Bronze Age (Southern Levant)
date_note: approx.; EB IV (Intermediate Bronze Age) c. 2500–2000
making_significance: Walled towns grew with trade in wine, oil and copper to Egypt, and EB IV saw a return to village life.
leaves_out: the pastoral groups of EB IV cast as "nomads"
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Middle Bronze Age (Levant)
making_significance: Canaanite city-states built rampart towns and made fast-wheel pottery, tin bronze and ivory furniture fittings.
leaves_out: competing MB labelling systems (MB I vs MB IIA)
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports; Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Late Bronze Age (Levant)
making_significance: Levantine ports such as Ugarit traded copper, tin, glass and purple dye across the eastern Mediterranean, and alphabetic scripts spread.
leaves_out: the collapse narrative's focus on elites
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports; Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Iron Age (Levant)
date_note: approx.; end at the Babylonian conquest of Judah
making_significance: Small kingdoms such as Israel, Judah, Moab and the Phoenician cities made ivories, inscribed seals and pottery.
leaves_out: the politics of biblical archaeology and whose sites get dug
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports; Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Early Bronze Age (Anatolia)
making_significance: Anatolian workshops made the Troy "treasures" and the Alaca Höyük standards in gold, silver and bronze.
leaves_out: the looted and dispersed finds
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports; Wikimedia Commons

name: Assyrian Colony period (Anatolia)
making_significance: Assyrian merchants at Kanesh traded tin and textiles for Anatolian silver, and local potters made beak-spouted jugs and animal vessels.
leaves_out: the Anatolian majority in Kanesh
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (link-out)

name: Iron Age (Anatolia)
making_significance: Phrygian, Neo-Hittite, Urartian and Lydian states made inlaid wooden furniture, bronze cauldrons and the first coins.
leaves_out: non-state groups
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports; Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Iron Age (southeastern Arabia)
making_significance: Communities in Oman and the UAE dug falaj channels, and made soft-stone vessels and bronze weapons.
leaves_out: the pastoral groups of the interior
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Late Pre-Islamic period (Arabia)
making_significance: Arabian towns such as Mleiha and ed-Dur minted coins, made glass and traded with Rome, Parthia and India.
leaves_out: nomadic and non-literate groups
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Jahiliyya
making_significance: Islamic tradition uses the label for pre-Islamic Arabia, hiding the written, built and crafted cultures of Saba, Nabataea and others.
leaves_out: the pre-Islamic Arabian makers
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out)

name: Late Bronze–Early Iron Age (South Caucasus)
making_significance: South Caucasian communities made bronze belts, wagons and weapons found in Lchashen and Metsamor burials.
leaves_out: the regional terminology
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Early Cycladic period
making_significance: Cycladic islanders carved marble figurines and vessels and made longboats, known mostly from looted graves.
leaves_out: the context lost to looting driven by the modern art market
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Middle Minoan period
making_significance: The first palaces made eggshell-thin Kamares ware on the fast wheel and early Cretan scripts.
leaves_out: non-palatial Crete
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports; Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Late Minoan period
making_significance: Later palaces made frescoes, marine-style pots and Linear A, then Linear B tablets under Mycenaean control.
leaves_out: Evans's reconstructions, now debated
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports; Wikimedia Commons

name: Late Helladic period
making_significance: Mycenaean palaces ran workshops for bronze, perfume, textiles and chariot parts recorded in Linear B.
leaves_out: the workers recorded in Linear B
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports; Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Early Iron Age (Greece)
making_significance: After the palace collapse, iron working spread and Lefkandi shows wealth and long-distance trade.
leaves_out: the "dark" label, contradicted by finds
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Geometric period (Greece)
making_significance: Athenian potters made large geometric grave markers, and the alphabet was adapted.
leaves_out: non-Attic workshops
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Archaic period (Greece)
date_note: approx.; start variously 776 or c. 700 BCE; end 480 BCE
making_significance: Greek city-states built stone temples, carved kouroi and korai, and Corinthian and Athenian potters developed black-figure painting for export.
leaves_out: the Phoenician, Egyptian and Anatolian sources of many techniques
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Classical period (Greece)
date_note: conventional; 480 (Persian Wars) to 323 BCE (death of Alexander)
making_significance: Athenian workshops made red-figure pottery, bronze statues and the Parthenon sculptures, later treated in Europe as the standard of art.
leaves_out: the enslaved and metic workers in Athenian workshops
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons
notes: links: STY004; POL117. "Classical" as norm is a F1.3 topic.

name: Hellenistic period
making_significance: Kingdoms founded after Alexander spread Greek workshops from Egypt to Bactria, with new work in glass, gems, bronze and mosaic.
defined_by: historians (term popularised by J. G. Droysen, 1836)
leaves_out: the Egyptian, Iranian and Indian makers who shaped "Greek" art
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Roman Republic
making_significance: The Republic expanded across the Mediterranean, and conquest brought Greek art, artists and enslaved craftworkers to Rome.
leaves_out: the enslaved people who did much of the craft work
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Roman Imperial period
date_note: 27 BCE to 476 CE in the West; East continues as Byzantium
making_significance: Empire-wide workshops made terra sigillata, glass, mosaics and concrete buildings.
leaves_out: provincial makers counted as "Roman"
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Late Antiquity
date_note: approx.; Peter Brown's "world of late antiquity"
making_significance: The label treats the late Roman, early Byzantine, Sasanian and early Islamic worlds as a continuous era of silk, mosaic, ivory and manuscript making.
leaves_out: the Germanic and steppe peoples cast as outsiders
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Early Byzantine period
date_note: approx.; 330 to the end of Iconoclasm
making_significance: Constantinople's workshops made Hagia Sophia, silk textiles, ivories and the earliest surviving icons.
leaves_out: the provinces and the Coptic, Syrian and Armenian makers
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Middle Byzantine period
making_significance: After Iconoclasm, enamel, ivory and icon workshops flourished and supplied Rus and Italy.
leaves_out: non-elite makers
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Late Byzantine period
making_significance: Palaiologan patrons commissioned mosaics and frescoes such as those of the Chora church.
leaves_out: Latin and Ottoman neighbours
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Upper Palaeolithic (Europe)
making_significance: Upper Palaeolithic people in Europe made cave paintings, carved ivory figurines, bone needles and blade tools.
defined_by: European prehistorians (Lartet and Christy; Breuil; de Mortillet)
leaves_out: older art and ornament from Africa and Asia that the "creative explosion" story overlooked
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Wikimedia Commons; open-access excavation reports
notes: links: ARC070; ARC071; ARC072; ARC073; INV154.

name: Mesolithic (northern Europe)
date_note: approx.; ends with farming, earlier in the south
making_significance: Post-glacial hunter-fishers made microliths, dugout canoes, fish traps and antler tools.
defined_by: European prehistorians (term from Hodder Westropp, 1866; later defined by Grahame Clark and others)
leaves_out: the persistence of foraging alongside farmers
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Three-age system (Stone, Bronze, Iron)
making_significance: Christian Jürgensen Thomsen arranged the Danish national collection by the material of tools, creating the Stone, Bronze and Iron Age sequence later applied far beyond the region it was built for.
defined_by: C. J. Thomsen (Guide to Northern Antiquities, 1836)
leaves_out: regions where copper, bronze and iron arrived in other orders or not at all (sub-Saharan Africa, Americas, Oceania)
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Internet Archive (public-domain texts)
notes: Always give the region when using these ages.

name: Copper Age (Balkans)
making_significance: Balkan communities mined and smelted copper and made the gold of the Varna cemetery.
leaves_out: the "Old Europe" label's romantic claims
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Bronze Age (Central Europe, Reinecke)
making_significance: Reinecke's scheme dates Central European bronze hoards, weapons and ornaments by type.
leaves_out: the people behind the types
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Europeana (per-item rights)

name: Bronze Age (Britain and Ireland)
making_significance: Metalworkers in Britain and Ireland made gold lunulae, bronze axes and beakers, trading tin and copper.
leaves_out: the continental migrants shown by aDNA
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports; Wikimedia Commons

name: Migration Period
making_significance: Migrating groups carried garnet cloisonné and animal-style metalwork across Europe.
leaves_out: the Roman population who stayed
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Europeana (per-item rights)

name: Viking Age
making_significance: Norse traders, raiders and settlers made ships, silver hoards and animal-style art from Kyiv to Greenland.
leaves_out: Sámi, Slavic and other partners
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Europeana (per-item rights)

name: Anglo-Saxon period
making_significance: Early English kingdoms made the Sutton Hoo gold and garnet work, the Lindisfarne Gospels and opus anglicanum embroidery.
leaves_out: the Britons and later Norse; the term's use by white-supremacist groups has led many scholars to prefer "early medieval England"
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Wikimedia Commons; British Library public-domain images (Flickr Commons)

name: Reconquista
date_note: contested label; traditional start at Covadonga (c. 718–722)
making_significance: The label presents eight centuries as a Christian recovery of Iberia and hides long periods of shared making, as in Mudéjar building and lustreware.
leaves_out: the Muslim and Jewish makers who stayed after conquest
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out)
notes: Contested label; links: STY015; POL153; POL154.

name: Early Middle Ages (Europe)
date_note: conventional; the term "Middle Ages" was coined by 15th-century humanists
making_significance: Monasteries and courts in western Europe made illuminated gospel books, reliquaries and metalwork, often using Mediterranean and eastern materials.
leaves_out: the Byzantine and Islamic worlds, where there was no "middle age"
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Wikimedia Commons; Europeana (per-item rights)

name: High Middle Ages (Europe)
making_significance: Growing towns built cathedrals and organised crafts into guilds, while stained glass, tapestry and enamel workshops served church and court.
leaves_out: women's and rural craft outside guilds
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Renaissance (Italy)
date_note: approx.; label from Michelet (1855) and Burckhardt (1860)
making_significance: The label casts Italian and later European art of c. 1400–1600 as a rebirth of antiquity, stressing named artists over workshops.
leaves_out: workshop assistants, women makers, and Islamic and Byzantine sources
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); National Gallery of Art (US) Open Access; Wikimedia Commons

name: Early modern period
making_significance: Historians use the term for the era of global maritime trade, print and early empires, now often applied beyond Europe.
defined_by: European historians, extended by global historians
leaves_out: societies whose histories do not fit the European turning points
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out)

name: Age of Discovery
other_names: Age of Exploration; Age of Contact
date_note: approx.; Ceuta 1415 often used as start
making_significance: The label celebrates European voyages that opened sea routes for trade in textiles, porcelain, silver and people, but names the period from the voyagers' side.
leaves_out: the peoples "discovered", and Asian and African sailors already on the routes
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Library of Congress (per-item rights; many public domain); Wikimedia Commons

name: Industrial Revolution (Britain)
date_note: approx.; term popularised by Arnold Toynbee's lectures (1881, publ. 1884)
making_significance: Water and steam power, coke-smelted iron and factory spinning moved much textile and metal making from homes and workshops into mills.
defined_by: economic historians (Toynbee; later debate on gradualism)
leaves_out: Indian and other textile industries it undercut, enslaved cotton growers, child workers
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Science Museum Group Collection (link-out); Yale Center for British Art (public-domain images)

name: Long nineteenth century
making_significance: Hobsbawm framed 1789–1914 as the age of revolution, capital and empire, during which industrial making and colonial extraction grew together.
leaves_out: non-European periodisations of the same years
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out)

name: Machine Age
date_note: approx.; label popular in the 1920s–30s (e.g. the 1927 Machine-Age Exposition, New York)
making_significance: Designers and artists of the interwar years celebrated machines and machine-made forms in streamlined and modernist products.
defined_by: design historians; the period's own promoters
leaves_out: the craft labour behind "machine-made" looks
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where designated); Library of Congress (per-item rights; many public domain)
notes: links: STY043; OCC209. Date span varies by author.

name: Cold War
making_significance: Rivalry between the US and USSR used design, exhibitions and craft as propaganda, from the "kitchen debate" to Soviet and US pavilions.
leaves_out: the hot wars fought in Asia, Africa and Latin America
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Library of Congress (per-item rights; many public domain)

name: Tatar yoke
making_significance: Russian historiography used the label for Golden Horde overlordship, hiding its trade and craft links with the steppe and Central Asia.
leaves_out: Golden Horde workshops and exchange
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out)

name: Tourkokratia
making_significance: Greek historiography calls the period of Ottoman rule "Turkish rule", which obscures shared crafts and Greek workshops across the empire.
leaves_out: Greek makers who prospered under Ottoman rule
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out)

name: Information Age
making_significance: Microprocessors, personal computers and networks moved design, publishing and much manufacturing control into software.
leaves_out: the mining and assembly labour behind devices
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out)

name: Anthropocene
date_note: proposed start c. 1950; formal epoch rejected by the IUGS in 2024
making_significance: Scientists proposed that humans now shape the Earth system enough to name a new epoch, with plastics, concrete and fallout as markers.
defined_by: Paul Crutzen and Eugene Stoermer (2000); Anthropocene Working Group (from 2009)
leaves_out: who caused the change; alternatives such as Capitalocene and Plantationocene
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access journals (DOAJ, SciELO, Persée)
notes: Contested label; formal proposal (Crawford Lake) rejected in March 2024.

name: Last Glacial Maximum
making_significance: At the coldest point of the last ice age, people made sewn clothing, used mammoth bone for shelters in Eastern Europe and occupied cold regions.
leaves_out: regional variation in timing
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access journals (DOAJ, SciELO, Persée)

name: Holocene
making_significance: The present warm epoch covers farming, cities, metals and almost all the making in this atlas.
leaves_out: the Anthropocene debate over whether it has ended
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access journals (DOAJ, SciELO, Persée)

name: Meghalayan Age
making_significance: A drought event about 4,200 years ago, used to define the latest Holocene stage, is linked by some to changes in Akkadian, Indus and Egyptian societies.
leaves_out: critics of climate-driven collapse stories
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access journals (DOAJ, SciELO, Persée)

name: Little Ice Age
making_significance: Colder centuries in parts of the Northern Hemisphere are linked by historians with harvest failures, frozen rivers and the end of Norse Greenland.
leaves_out: regional variation and the debate on causes
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access journals (DOAJ, SciELO, Persée)

name: Xia (contested period)
date_note: traditional; dates from the Xia–Shang–Zhou Chronology Project (2000)
making_significance: Chinese historiography places a Xia dynasty before the Shang, and some archaeologists identify it with Erlitou's bronze-casting centre, though no Xia writing has been found.
defined_by: traditional Chinese historiography (Sima Qian); Xia–Shang–Zhou Chronology Project
leaves_out: the many other Late Neolithic centres the dynastic line leaves out
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Spring and Autumn period
date_note: conventional; named after the Chunqiu annals
making_significance: Rival Zhou states cast inscribed ritual bronzes with new pattern-block methods and began iron use.
leaves_out: non-Zhou peoples such as the Rong and Yi
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0)

name: Warring States period
making_significance: Competing states mass-produced iron tools and crossbows, made lacquerware, silk and inlaid bronzes, and wrote the Kaogongji on crafts.
leaves_out: the conscript and convict labour in state workshops
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0)

name: Six Dynasties
date_note: conventional; the six southern capitals at Jiankang
making_significance: Southern courts developed calligraphy, painting theory and celadon, while Buddhism brought cave temples in the north.
leaves_out: the northern dynasties, the term centres the south
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0)

name: Northern Song period
making_significance: From Kaifeng, the Song court and markets made Ru, Ding and Jun wares, printed books and the Yingzao fashi building manual.
leaves_out: the Liao and Xi Xia, who shared its technologies
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data (CC BY 4.0); Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0)

name: Southern Song period
making_significance: From Hangzhou the court supported Longquan celadon, Guan ware, academy painting and a large maritime trade.
leaves_out: the Jin in the north
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data (CC BY 4.0); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Transitional period (Chinese porcelain)
making_significance: During the Ming–Qing wars, Jingdezhen potters made blue-and-white with new narrative scenes for private and export buyers.
leaves_out: the potters' conditions during the wars
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Rijksmuseum (CC0/PDM)

name: High Qing
making_significance: Under the Kangxi, Yongzheng and Qianlong emperors, palace workshops made enamels, porcelain, jade and glass.
leaves_out: the Taiwanese, Tibetan and Xinjiang conquests of the same years
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data (CC BY 4.0); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Century of Humiliation
making_significance: The label frames the Opium Wars to 1949 as foreign humiliation, a frame that shapes PRC restitution demands such as for the Yuanmingyuan bronzes.
leaves_out: Chinese modernisation from within
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out)

name: Republican period (China)
making_significance: The Republic brought art schools, modern printing, advertising posters and new dress such as the qipao.
leaves_out: rural makers and warlord regions
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out)

name: Mao era
making_significance: State planning organised crafts into co-operatives and produced propaganda posters and export crafts.
leaves_out: the famine and persecution of makers
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out)

name: Reform era (China)
making_significance: Economic reform turned coastal China into a centre of export manufacture and revived private craft.
leaves_out: migrant workers
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out)

name: Imperial reign eras (nianhao) as dating units
date_note: first era name 140 BCE, or c. 110 BCE in other sources; Chinese use ended 1912; Japan still uses nengō
making_significance: Reign marks such as "Da Ming Chenghua nian zhi" date porcelain and other wares, and are copied on later pieces.
defined_by: Chinese, Korean, Vietnamese and Japanese courts
leaves_out: makers who copied marks as homage
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data (CC BY 4.0)

name: Era of Fragmentation (Tibet)
making_significance: After the Tibetan empire broke up, monasteries lost royal patronage, and Buddhist making revived later with the "later spread".
leaves_out: local Bon and lay traditions the Buddhist frame hides
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out)

name: Later spread of Buddhism (Tibet)
making_significance: Monasteries such as Tabo and Alchi were built and painted with help from Kashmiri and Indian craftsmen.
leaves_out: the lay patrons and Kashmiri artists
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Palaeolithic (Japan)
making_significance: People in Japan made edge-ground stone axes and blade tools, among the earliest ground-stone tools known.
leaves_out: the 2000 hoax (Fujimura) that faked older sites
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Incipient Jōmon
date_note: approx.; calibrated dates vary by author
making_significance: Foragers in Japan made small, round- or pointed-based pots with linear-relief and cord decoration, among the oldest known pottery anywhere.
leaves_out: the separate dates for Hokkaido and the Ryukyus
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms)

name: Initial Jōmon
making_significance: More settled communities made pointed-base cord-marked pots for boiling and left the first large shell middens.
leaves_out: variation between regional pottery types
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms)

name: Early Jōmon
making_significance: Red lacquered combs and bowls from wet sites such as Torihama show lacquer use, alongside flat-based pots and plant-fibre cordage.
leaves_out: the women potters inferred but rarely named in accounts
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms)

name: Middle Jōmon
making_significance: Large villages such as Sannai-Maruyama built large timber buildings and made clay figurines, while flame-rimmed pots were made in the Shinano River basin.
leaves_out: the modern nationalist use of Jōmon as "original Japanese"
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms); Japan Search

name: Late Jōmon
making_significance: Communities built stone circles in the north and made finer lacquered wares, earplugs and spouted vessels.
leaves_out: the Ainu link to northern Jōmon descendants
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms)

name: Final Jōmon
date_note: approx.; lasts later in northern Japan
making_significance: The Kamegaoka culture of northern Japan made goggle-eyed figurines and fine lacquered pottery as rice farming began in Kyushu.
leaves_out: its overlap with early Yayoi in western Japan
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms); Japan Search

name: Yayoi period
date_note: start revised to c. 1000–900 BCE by AMS dating (National Museum of Japanese History, 2003); older texts say c. 300 BCE
making_significance: Rice farming, bronze bells and mirrors, iron tools and wheel-less red pottery arrived with migrants from the Korean peninsula.
defined_by: Japanese historiography (named after the Yayoi-chō site in Tokyo, 1884)
leaves_out: the Jōmon people of the north who kept foraging, and the Korean origin of many techniques
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Kofun period
making_significance: Rulers were buried in keyhole-shaped mounds ringed with haniwa figures and filled with iron armour, mirrors and stoneware made with Korean techniques.
leaves_out: the Korean immigrant makers (toraijin) who brought many techniques
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Asuka period
making_significance: Buddhism and Korean and Chinese builders brought temple architecture, gilt-bronze images and roof tiles to the Yamato court.
leaves_out: the Baekje craftsmen credited only as a group
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms)

name: Nara period
making_significance: The court at Heijō-kyō cast the Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji and stored imported and local treasures in the Shōsōin.
leaves_out: the corvée labourers who cast the Great Buddha
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms)

name: Heian period
making_significance: The Kyoto court made kana calligraphy, narrative handscrolls, lacquer with maki-e and Pure Land temples such as the Byōdō-in.
leaves_out: provincial and non-aristocratic life
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Kamakura period
making_significance: The shogunate's era saw Kei school sculpture, Zen temple building and Seto glazed stoneware.
leaves_out: the imperial court in Kyoto
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms)

name: Muromachi period
making_significance: Ashikaga patronage supported ink painting, Noh masks, the tea ceremony and trade with Ming China.
leaves_out: the rural and Ryukyuan worlds
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Sengoku period
making_significance: Constant war brought castle building, mass production of guns after 1543 and armour for foot soldiers.
leaves_out: the people displaced by war
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms)

name: Azuchi–Momoyama period
making_significance: Nobunaga and Hideyoshi commissioned gold-leaf screens, castles and tea wares.
leaves_out: the Korean potters brought by force
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Edo period
making_significance: Under Tokugawa rule, urban markets supported woodblock prints, textiles, lacquer and porcelain for domestic and export buyers.
leaves_out: the Ainu, Ryukyuans and outcaste groups (burakumin) who did leather and other crafts
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms); Met Open Access (CC0); Art Institute of Chicago (CC0 public-domain works)

name: Meiji period
making_significance: The Meiji state industrialised, sent crafts to world's fairs, founded art schools and museums, and redirected sword and temple makers to export goods.
leaves_out: the Ainu and Ryukyuans absorbed by the state, and the women in silk mills
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms); Met Open Access (CC0); NDL Digital Collections (public-domain items)

name: Taishō period
making_significance: Urban consumer culture brought department stores, modern design, sōsaku-hanga prints and the start of the Mingei circle.
leaves_out: colonised Korea and Taiwan, whose makers served the empire
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); NDL Digital Collections (public-domain items)

name: Shōwa period
making_significance: The era runs from militarism and war through occupation to the post-war boom in cameras, electronics and cars and the Living National Treasures system.
leaves_out: the wartime forced labour of Koreans and Chinese
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); NDL Digital Collections (public-domain items)

name: Epi-Jōmon (Hokkaido)
making_significance: Hokkaido foragers kept making cord-marked pottery while rice farming spread in the south.
leaves_out: the ancestors of the Ainu
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Ainu culture period
making_significance: Ainu made elm-bark cloth (attus), appliqué robes and ritual inau carvings, and traded with Japanese and the Amur region.
leaves_out: the Ainu present, which "period" can hide
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms)
notes: Label contested; Ainu culture continues today.

name: Gusuku period
making_significance: Local lords in Okinawa built stone gusuku fortresses and traded with China, leading to the Ryukyu Kingdom.
leaves_out: the commoners and the northern Amami islands
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Gojoseon (contested period)
date_note: traditional founding 2333 BCE from later texts; historical from c. 4th century BCE
making_significance: Korean tradition dates Gojoseon's founding to 2333 BCE, while archaeology links the later state with mandolin-shaped bronze daggers and dolmens.
leaves_out: the many non-Gojoseon groups on the peninsula
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); KOGL Type 1 images on Wikimedia Commons

name: Proto-Three Kingdoms period
making_significance: Iron production in the south of Korea supplied iron ingots and armour traded to Japan.
leaves_out: the chiefdoms not named in Chinese texts
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); KOGL Type 1 images on Wikimedia Commons

name: Three Kingdoms period (Korea)
date_note: traditional founding dates from the Samguk sagi (1145)
making_significance: Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla (with Gaya) made tomb murals, gold crowns and Buddhist sculpture, and sent craftsmen to Japan.
leaves_out: Gaya, left out of "three"
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); KOGL Type 1 images on Wikimedia Commons; Korean national e-museum (KOGL Type 1 items only)

name: Unified Silla period
making_significance: Unified Silla built the Seokguram grotto and Bulguksa temple and cast large bronze bells such as the Divine Bell of King Seongdeok.
leaves_out: Balhae in the north, which the term sets aside
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); KOGL Type 1 images on Wikimedia Commons

name: North–South States period
making_significance: The label pairs Silla with Balhae in Manchuria, whose Buddhist and tile work is otherwise left out of Korean history.
leaves_out: the Chinese and Russian claims to Balhae
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out)

name: Goryeo period
making_significance: Goryeo potters made inlaid celadon, and printers carved the Tripitaka Koreana and cast metal type.
leaves_out: the Mongol overlordship's share
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); KOGL Type 1 images on Wikimedia Commons; Korean national e-museum (KOGL Type 1 items only)

name: Joseon period
making_significance: Joseon court workshops made white porcelain and buncheong ware, state painters recorded rituals in uigwe, and Hangul was created.
leaves_out: the lowborn (cheonmin) artisans and slaves (nobi)
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); KOGL Type 1 images on Wikimedia Commons; Korean national e-museum (KOGL Type 1 items only); Kyujanggak / Uigwe (link-out)

name: Japanese colonial period (Korea)
making_significance: Colonial rule set up industrial exhibitions, museums and Korean craft revivals under Japanese direction, while taking many artworks to Japan.
leaves_out: Korean agency within colonial structures
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); KOGL Type 1 images on Wikimedia Commons

name: Bắc thuộc
making_significance: Vietnamese historiography names the centuries under Chinese rule as "northern domination", during which Đông Sơn bronze drums gave way to Han-style tombs and ceramics.
leaves_out: the mixed Viet-Chinese elites
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Indus Tradition eras (Regionalisation, Integration, Localisation)
date_note: Regionalisation c. 5000–2600; Integration c. 2600–1900; Localisation c. 1900–1300 BCE
making_significance: Jim Shaffer's scheme replaces "rise and fall" with eras of regional styles, an integrated phase of standard weights, seals and beads, and a return to regional crafts.
leaves_out: the Indus script, still unread, so makers' own terms are unknown
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); open-access excavation reports
notes: links: ARC138; ARC139; ARC140; CIV048; INV173.

name: Vedic period
date_note: approx.; early and later Vedic phases
making_significance: The period of the Vedic texts is linked by many archaeologists with Painted Grey Ware, iron and fire-altar building.
materials_techniques: iron smelting;Painted Grey Ware;brick altar building
leaves_out: non-Vedic peoples and the Indus heritage; the date debate shaped by nationalism
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Early Historic period (South Asia)
making_significance: Towns and states of the Ganges plain issued punch-marked coins, made Northern Black Polished Ware and built Buddhist stupas.
leaves_out: the tribal and forest peoples outside the towns
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Mauryan period
making_significance: The Maurya empire carved polished sandstone pillars with Ashoka's edicts and animal capitals.
leaves_out: the Persian and Hellenistic sources of pillar techniques, a debated question
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Sangam period
making_significance: Tamil poetry of the period describes ports, weavers and gem workers, confirmed by finds at Arikamedu and Keezhadi.
leaves_out: the dating debate and non-Tamil groups
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Gupta period
making_significance: Gupta-era workshops made Buddhist and Hindu sculpture, the Ajanta murals and iron such as the Delhi pillar.
leaves_out: the Vakatakas and others who made much of the art credited to Guptas
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons
notes: links: POL188; STY118; DYN041. "Golden age" is contested.

name: Early medieval period (India)
making_significance: Regional kingdoms built temples in stone and bronze, with guilds and temple towns as centres of making.
leaves_out: forest and tribal peoples
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Sultanate period (India)
making_significance: Sultanate rule brought new building (true arches, domes), paper and textile workshops to north India.
leaves_out: regional sultanates and Rajput kingdoms
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Mughal period
making_significance: Mughal court workshops (karkhanas) made painting, carpets, jade, jewelled arms and buildings such as the Taj Mahal.
leaves_out: non-court makers and the Deccan and Rajput courts
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0)

name: Colonial period (South Asia)
making_significance: Company and Crown rule collapsed some textile trades, set up art schools and museums, and later met Swadeshi and khadi campaigns.
leaves_out: princely states and the makers' own resistance
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); British Library public-domain images (Flickr Commons); Indian Culture portal (per-owner licence)

name: Mill's periodisation (Hindu, Muslim, British)
date_note: James Mill, History of British India (1817)
making_significance: Mill divided India's past into Hindu, Muslim and British periods, a religious framing that still shapes museums and textbooks.
leaves_out: Buddhist, Jain, tribal and syncretic makers; continuities across the periods
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Internet Archive (public-domain texts)

name: Kali Yuga
date_note: traditional start 3102 BCE; ongoing in Puranic reckoning
making_significance: In Puranic cosmology the present age began in 3102 BCE, a cyclical time frame different from archaeological periods.
leaves_out: non-Hindu traditions
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out)

name: Polonnaruwa period
making_significance: Sri Lankan kings at Polonnaruwa carved the Gal Vihara Buddhas and built reservoirs.
leaves_out: the Chola rule that began it
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Licchavi period (Nepal)
making_significance: Licchavi kings in the Kathmandu Valley made stone sculpture and inscribed stelae.
leaves_out: non-royal makers
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Pre-Angkorian period
making_significance: Early Khmer kingdoms carved Hindu and Buddhist stone images and built brick temples.
leaves_out: the Chinese-derived names Funan and Chenla
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Angkorian period
making_significance: Khmer kings built Angkor's temples, reservoirs and canals and cast bronze images, with the labour listed in temple inscriptions.
leaves_out: the bonded temple labourers recorded in the inscriptions
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Post-Angkorian period
making_significance: Khmer courts moved south, and wooden and lacquered Buddhist images replaced stone.
leaves_out: the "dark age" label
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out)

name: Classical (Hindu-Buddhist) period (Indonesia)
making_significance: Javanese kingdoms built Borobudur and Prambanan and cast bronze and gold images, while Srivijaya on Sumatra traded across the region.
leaves_out: the Islamic and local continuities that the Indic label hides
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Rijksmuseum (CC0/PDM); Tropenmuseum images on Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

name: Rattanakosin period
making_significance: The Chakri court in Bangkok made lacquer, mother-of-pearl and mural painting.
leaves_out: non-Thai peoples
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out)

name: Age of Commerce (Southeast Asia)
making_significance: Reid described Southeast Asian port cities thriving on trade in spices, textiles and ceramics.
leaves_out: the hinterland
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out)

name: Rashidun period
making_significance: The first caliphs kept Byzantine and Sasanian coin types and craft workshops running in the conquered provinces.
leaves_out: Shiʿi readings of the same years
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Umayyad period
making_significance: Umayyad rulers built the Dome of the Rock and desert palaces, and created an epigraphic coinage.
leaves_out: Byzantine and Coptic craftsmen who did much of the work
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Abbasid period
making_significance: From Baghdad and Samarra, Abbasid workshops made lustreware, paper, bookbinding and stucco.
leaves_out: the regional dynasties that ruled in practice
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0)

name: Islamic Golden Age
making_significance: The label praises science and craft under the Abbasids but implies a later decline that historians reject.
leaves_out: Ottoman, Safavid, Mughal and later achievements
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out)

name: Hodgson's Middle Periods
date_note: Marshall Hodgson, The Venture of Islam (1974)
making_significance: Hodgson's periods cover the Seljuk, Mongol and Timurid worlds of craft and trade.
leaves_out: non-Persianate regions
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out)

name: Timurid Renaissance
making_significance: The label frames Timurid court painting, tilework and bookmaking as a rebirth.
leaves_out: the deported craftsmen
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Gunpowder Empires
making_significance: Hodgson and McNeill grouped the Ottomans, Safavids and Mughals around guns.
leaves_out: court workshops that the gun frame ignores
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out)

name: Ottoman Classical Age
date_note: İnalcık's scheme covers 1300–1600; art historians often focus on c. 1520–1600
making_significance: In İnalcık's scheme the empire's classical centuries culminate in court workshops making İznik tiles, saz-style designs and the mosques of the architect Sinan.
leaves_out: provincial makers and non-Muslim craft communities
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Late Bronze Age (Eurasian steppe)
making_significance: Steppe herders of the Sintashta and Andronovo horizons made spoked-wheel chariots, tin bronzes and fortified settlements.
leaves_out: the idea of a single "Aryan" people, which the label has been used to support
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Early Nomadic period (Eurasian steppe)
making_significance: Mounted nomads made gold animal-style ornaments, felts and tattooed textiles preserved in frozen kurgans such as Pazyryk.
leaves_out: the settled neighbours on whom nomads depended
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports; Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Pax Mongolica
making_significance: The label stresses safe trade under Mongol rule, when silk, porcelain and ideas moved across Eurasia.
leaves_out: the violence of conquest and deportations
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0)

name: Soviet period (Central Asia)
making_significance: Soviet rule collectivised herding and crafts, built cotton monocultures and organised state craft cooperatives and design institutes.
leaves_out: nomads' own sense of the period
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out)

name: Paleoindian period (Americas)
date_note: approx.; pre-Clovis sites push the start earlier
making_significance: The first peoples of the Americas made fluted points such as Clovis, and pre-Clovis sites are still debated.
leaves_out: oral histories of Indigenous origins
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Archaic period (Mesoamerica)
making_significance: Foragers domesticated maize, squash and beans and began to make ground-stone tools.
leaves_out: variation between highlands and lowlands
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Early Formative period (Mesoamerica)
making_significance: Villages made pottery, figurines and, on the Gulf Coast, Olmec monumental stone heads.
leaves_out: non-Olmec regions
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); INAH Mediateca (link-out)

name: Middle Formative period (Mesoamerica)
making_significance: Jade carving, early writing and ceremonial centres such as La Venta and early Maya sites developed.
leaves_out: small villages
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Late Formative period (Mesoamerica)
making_significance: Large Maya cities such as El Mirador and early Teotihuacan built stucco-masked pyramids.
leaves_out: highland Oaxacan developments
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Early Classic period (Mesoamerica)
making_significance: Teotihuacan's workshops made obsidian tools, Thin Orange pottery and murals while Maya kings raised dated stelae.
leaves_out: the non-Maya regions, fitted to a Maya-defined "classic"
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); INAH Mediateca (link-out)

name: Late Classic period (Mesoamerica)
making_significance: Maya courts produced painted polychrome vessels, carved lintels and scribal art signed by named painters.
leaves_out: commoners and non-royal makers
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); INAH Mediateca (link-out)

name: Terminal Classic period (Mesoamerica)
making_significance: Southern Maya cities were abandoned while northern Yucatán cities such as Uxmal grew.
leaves_out: northern growth hidden by "collapse"
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out)

name: Early Postclassic period (Mesoamerica)
making_significance: Tula and Chichén Itzá used columned halls and began metalworking from West Mexico.
leaves_out: smaller polities
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out)

name: Late Postclassic period (Mesoamerica)
making_significance: Mixtec, Aztec and other states made codices, turquoise mosaic, gold and featherwork.
leaves_out: non-Aztec peoples
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); INAH Mediateca (link-out)

name: Colonial period (Spanish America)
making_significance: Indigenous, African and European makers created silver, textiles, painting and featherwork under Spanish rule.
leaves_out: Indigenous and African agency
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); INAH Mediateca (link-out)

name: Preceramic Period (Andes)
making_significance: Before pottery, Andean people made twined cotton textiles, gourd containers and the monumental centres of Caral and Norte Chico.
leaves_out: the forager and herder communities of the highlands
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Initial Period (Andes)
making_significance: Pottery and heddle-loom weaving spread, and coastal U-shaped temple complexes were built.
leaves_out: the scheme's roots in one coastal valley (Ica)
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Early Horizon (period)
making_significance: The period of the Chavín style saw goldwork, painted textiles and stone carving spread across the Andes.
leaves_out: the regional cultures that were not Chavín
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0)
notes: links: HOR001; STY064; CIV032. Period row; HOR001 is the horizon as stylistic spread.

name: Early Intermediate Period
making_significance: Regional cultures such as Moche and Nasca made moulded portrait vessels, gold and copper alloys and embroidered and painted textiles.
leaves_out: the "intermediate" framing as a gap between horizons
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0)

name: Middle Horizon (period)
making_significance: Wari and Tiwanaku spread tapestry tunics, stone architecture and a shared imagery across the Andes.
leaves_out: local communities under Wari and Tiwanaku
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0)

name: Late Intermediate Period
making_significance: Regional states such as Chimor made mould-made blackware, feather and textile work and sheet metal.
leaves_out: the "intermediate" framing
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0)

name: Late Horizon (period)
date_note: approx.; based on Spanish-recorded Inca chronology
making_significance: Inca rule organised state weaving (qompi), metalwork, fine stone masonry and khipu records.
leaves_out: the conquered peoples' own histories
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Met Open Access (CC0)
notes: links: HOR003; POL061; STY066; INV005. Labour tribute (mit'a) flagged.

name: Lumbreras's developmental periodisation
other_names: Formative, Regional Development, Wari Empire, Regional States, Tawantinsuyu
making_significance: Lumbreras's Marxist scheme orders Andean history by social stages rather than by stylistic horizons.
leaves_out: the variation within stages
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out)

name: Archaic period (Eastern North America)
making_significance: Foragers made ground-stone tools, bannerstones, early mounds and copper tools.
leaves_out: the living nations who descend from these people
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Woodland period
making_significance: Woodland peoples made pottery, burial mounds and Hopewell's mica, copper and pipe work.
leaves_out: the nations who descend from these people
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Mississippian period
making_significance: Mound centres such as Cahokia made shell gorgets, copper plates and ceramics.
leaves_out: the living nations
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Basketmaker II
making_significance: Early maize farmers on the Colorado Plateau made coiled and twined baskets, sandals and atlatls, but little pottery.
leaves_out: Pueblo peoples' own histories and the name "Anasazi" they reject
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Basketmaker III
making_significance: Pit-house villages adopted fired pottery, the bow and arrow and beans, alongside continuing fine basketry.
leaves_out: Pueblo oral history
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Pueblo I
making_significance: Above-ground pueblo roomblocks appeared, with neck-banded grey and black-on-white pottery.
leaves_out: Pueblo oral history
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Pueblo II
making_significance: Chaco Canyon's great houses, road network and turquoise working flourished across the San Juan Basin.
leaves_out: Pueblo oral history
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Pueblo III
making_significance: Pueblo peoples gathered into large villages and cliff dwellings such as those at Mesa Verde after the Chaco great-house system of Pueblo II declined.
leaves_out: the "abandonment" framing Pueblos reject
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Pueblo IV
making_significance: Large pueblos made glaze-painted pottery and kiva murals and developed katsina imagery.
leaves_out: Pueblo oral history
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Pueblo V
making_significance: Pueblo peoples continued to make pottery, weaving and katsina figures under Spanish, Mexican and US rule.
leaves_out: living Pueblo communities who are not "prehistory"
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where designated)

name: Paleo-Inuit period (Arctic)
making_significance: Paleo-Inuit peoples of the Arctic Small Tool tradition, Saqqaq and Dorset made microblades and carved ivory figures.
defined_by: Arctic archaeologists; terminology revised after Inuit Circumpolar Council resolution (2010)
leaves_out: the Inuit terms for these peoples (e.g. Tuniit)
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Contact period (North America)
making_significance: The term marks Indigenous history by the arrival of Europeans and trade goods such as glass beads and copper kettles, which makers reworked into their own forms.
leaves_out: the continuity of Indigenous histories across the divide
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out)

name: Reservation period (Plains)
making_significance: Confined to reservations, Plains artists made ledger drawings, beadwork and quillwork for trade.
leaves_out: Native self-determination
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where designated)

name: Lithic Age (Caribbean)
making_significance: Rouse's first age covers the earliest Caribbean settlers, who made flaked-stone blades and tools.
leaves_out: later revisions that merge Lithic and Archaic
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Archaic Age (Caribbean)
making_significance: Rouse's second age covers foragers who made ground-stone and shell tools, though some also made early pottery and grew plants.
leaves_out: the evidence of early pottery and farming that blurs the age boundaries
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Early Ceramic Age (Caribbean)
making_significance: Saladoid migrants from South America brought white-on-red pottery, farming and carved stone and shell amulets.
leaves_out: the Archaic peoples already on the islands
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Late Ceramic Age (Caribbean)
making_significance: Ancestors of the Taíno carved zemís and duhos and built ball courts and plazas.
leaves_out: the living Taíno and other descendant communities
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Amazon rubber boom
making_significance: The rubber trade enslaved and killed Indigenous people and funded Manaus's opera house.
leaves_out: the Indigenous tappers and the debt-bonded migrants from Brazil's northeast
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); BNDigital (Biblioteca Nacional do Brasil)

name: Pleistocene Sahul
date_note: approx.; first settlement dated c. 65,000–50,000 years ago (debated)
making_significance: People crossed open sea to reach the joined landmass of Australia and New Guinea, making ground-edge axes, ochre pigments and shell beads.
leaves_out: Aboriginal and Papuan accounts of deep time that do not use "periods"
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Holocene intensification (Australia)
making_significance: Harry Lourandos argued that late Holocene Australia saw more complex fish traps, eel farms, small tools and exchange, challenging the idea of an unchanging "Stone Age" people.
leaves_out: Aboriginal knowledge holders' own chronology
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Frontier Wars period (Australia)
making_significance: Colonial violence and dispossession took land and materials from Aboriginal makers, while objects were collected for museums.
leaves_out: those who deny the wars
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Trove (link-out)

name: Lapita period
making_significance: Lapita potters made dentate-stamped pottery as they settled from the Bismarcks to Samoa.
leaves_out: the Papuan peoples already in Near Oceania
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports
notes: links: ARC224; HOR013; CIV091; NET046. Period row.

name: Long Pause (West Polynesia)
making_significance: After the settlement of Tonga and Samoa, a long gap before East Polynesian voyaging is argued by some archaeologists.
leaves_out: Polynesian navigational history
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: East Polynesian settlement phase
making_significance: Polynesian voyagers settled the Society Islands, Hawaiʻi, Rapa Nui and Aotearoa in a rapid series of voyages.
leaves_out: Polynesian genealogies and voyaging knowledge
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Archaic phase (Māori)
making_significance: The first Māori made adzes, fish-hooks and ornaments like those of East Polynesia.
leaves_out: Māori tribal histories that do not use Golson's phases
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Te Papa Collections Online (per-item; taonga restricted)

name: Classic phase (Māori)
making_significance: Māori built fortified pā, carved storehouses and meeting-house elements, and worked pounamu into hei-tiki and weapons.
leaves_out: Māori tribal histories that do not use Golson's phases
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); Te Papa Collections Online (per-item; taonga restricted)

name: Ahu Moai phase (Rapa Nui)
date_note: approx.; phase of the older culture-historical sequence, ended c. 1680 by a 'Huri Moai' toppling phase; recent dating finds ahu building from the 13th c. continuing past European contact (1722) and no pre-contact Huri Moai phase
making_significance: Rapa Nui people carved hundreds of moai at the Rano Raraku quarry and moved them to stone platforms (ahu).
defined_by: archaeologists (older culture-historical sequence; revised by DiNapoli, Lipo, Hunt et al.)
leaves_out: Rapa Nui accounts, and the debated 'collapse' story
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports

name: Latte period (Marianas)
making_significance: Chamorro communities in the Marianas quarried and raised latte stone pillars as house foundations.
leaves_out: Chamorro views of their own history
free_sources: PeriodO (period gazetteer; link-out); open-access excavation reports
